claims.text: Applying a phase-selective recrystallization heat treatment to an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy will simultaneously increase its strength and ductility.
The simultaneous improvement arises from optimized strain or load partitioning between a recrystallized soft FCC phase and an intact hard B2 or intermetallic phase.
As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloys can possess a fine lamellar FCC/B2 microstructure.
AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is an eutectic high-entropy alloy containing FCC and B2 phases.
Al0.7CoCrFeNi is an example of the stated fine-lamellar FCC/B2 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
In the dual-phase EHEA, the FCC phase is ductile and the B2 phase is strong.
The intervention can fully recrystallize the soft FCC phase while preserving a connected skeleton of the hard phase.
A temperature-time regime can be selected that fully recrystallizes the FCC phase without coarsening or changing the morphology of the B2 phase.
Processing under an inert atmosphere will prevent oxidation.
A dual-phase lamellar microstructure with robust phase boundaries can optimize strain partitioning.
Selective recrystallization homogenizes the ductile phase and sharpens the interface between the soft and hard phases.
The phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure improves strain partitioning and releases the strain-hardening capacity of both phases by eliminating weak boundaries.
The intact B2 phase retains high load-bearing capacity while the recrystallized FCC phase improves plasticity.
Improved strain distribution and stronger interfaces delay crack initiation along weak interfaces.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the treatment will increase both yield strength and ultimate tensile strength, potentially approaching or exceeding about 2 GPa.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the treatment will improve uniform elongation to approximately 35%.
The unmodified as-cast baseline has limited ductility because of weak boundaries and premature crack propagation.
Coarsening or loss of connectivity of the hard phase may negate the strength-ductility benefit.
The magnitude of improvement and the optimal heat-treatment parameters depend on alloy composition and processing details.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing as-cast and treated samples using tensile tests, EBSD/TEM microstructural characterization, and fracture-surface analysis.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that benefits are expected only when B2 morphology and connectivity are preserved, but the falsification rule treats excessive coarsening or compromised phase integrity as falsifying the hypothesis. Such an outcome is a failure to satisfy the stated intervention condition rather than a decisive test of the conditional hypothesis.
